tagline: An old turnpike links Harwinton’s town center and an agricultural crossroads.
intro: Harwinton’s scenic road follows Route 118 into the town center, then Route 4 east to Rock Brook. Connecticut designated the 1.51-mile Route 4 section in 1996; it connects with a scenic tenth of a mile on Route 118. At the central crossroads, houses sit back from the roads among churches and municipal buildings. Most of the historic district’s buildings date to the 19th century.

The Litchfield and Harwinton Turnpike company received its charter in October 1798 to improve and maintain the road linking Litchfield, Harwinton and Burlington. Its alignment followed modern Route 118 and continued along what is now Route 4. In 1963, Route 4 moved to its present alignment, shortening Route 116 to Harwinton. Three years later, that remaining road became Route 118. The number changed because a highway in Ridgefield needed 116 to match its connecting route across the New York line.

Traveling west to east, Litchfield Road reaches the Route 4 junction in Harwinton center and continues beyond it as Route 4. North and South Roads meet the east-west road at the traditional town center. Farther east, Harmony Hill Road and Locust Road mark the agricultural crossroads once called Catlin’s Corners. The scenic section ends at Rock Brook.

moments.title: Harwinton center
moments.text: Harwinton’s first meetinghouse stood directly in the central road junction. The town center grew where the Hartford-Litchfield road crossed the local north-south route, now North and South Roads. The district includes four churches and predominantly 19th-century buildings, with houses spaced well back from the roads. The Congregational Church is a simplified recreation of an 1808 sanctuary that burned in 1949. The Classical Revival library belongs to the early 20th century, another period represented at this crossroads. The district stretches along Route 4 between Birge Park Road and Harwinton Heights Road, with a branch down South Road.
moments.notice: Look for the Classical Revival library and the Congregational Church, a recreation of the lost 1808 sanctuary.

moments.title: South Road
moments.text: Quarry-stone walls along South Road came with Harwinton’s early-20th-century turn toward second homes. William McConway of Pittsburgh had them built. During the preceding century, the town had remained agricultural, without the railroad connections and suitable water resources needed for industrialization. The historic district follows South Road as far as Village Lane.

moments.title: Catlin’s Corners
moments.text: Two 18th-century houses built by Abijah Catlin define the intersection at Catlin’s Corners. His father, Abraham, operated a small shop, and the crossroads took his name. The settlement developed as a line of houses along Harmony Hill Road, with six built before the 19th century and a school added in the late 18th century. Later adaptations gave older buildings new roles: two houses were converted from barns, and another from the school. Wood-frame houses, typically two and a half stories tall, occupy well-spaced properties within the 103-acre historic district in eastern Harwinton.
